p1.key: If a reaction goes to completion the equilibrium lies far to the right, so product concentrations are much greater than reactant concentrations and Kc ≫ 1.

A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium position does not change. Higher pressure (fewer gas moles on the right), more O<sub>2</sub> and lower temperature (exothermic forward) all increase [SO<sub>3</sub>].

K<sub>c</sub> = products over reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient: [CS<sub>2</sub>][H<sub>2</sub>]<sup>4</sup> / [CH<sub>4</sub>][H<sub>2</sub>S]<sup>2</sup>. Coefficients are powers, not multipliers.
At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions keep going at equal rates, so reactants and products keep reacting while concentrations stay constant. K and the rates do not change.

Decreasing the volume raises the pressure and shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (2SO3). A higher temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, and a catalyst does not shift the equilibrium: II only.
Higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (SO3), raising the ratio. The forward reaction is exothermic, so higher temperature lowers the ratio: pressure only.
Kw increases with temperature, so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right. That means the forward ionization is endothermic. [H3O+] = [OH−] at every temperature.
K<sub>c</sub> = [NH<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2</sup>/([N<sub>2</sub>][H<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3</sup>). The coefficients become powers.
K<sub>c</sub> = [CH<sub>3</sub>OH]/([H<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2</sup>[CO]): products on top, coefficients as powers.
Higher pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (2NH3). The forward reaction is exothermic, so higher temperature shifts it left: I only.

At the new equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal again, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant. They need not be equal to each other, and K<sub>c</sub> need not be greater than 1.

Removing NH<sub>3</sub> lowers the product concentration, so the equilibrium shifts right to replace it. Higher temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, lower pressure favours the side with more gas moles, and a catalyst has no effect on position.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway that lowers the activation energy of both the forward and the reverse reactions equally. ΔH and the equilibrium position are unchanged.
At first there is no bromine vapour, so evaporation happens faster than condensation. As the vapour builds up, the condensation rate rises until the two rates are equal (equilibrium).
A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both directions, so the forward and reverse rates increase equally. Equilibrium is reached faster but its position, and so the yield, does not change.
Kc = [NO2]2/[N2O4], so [NO2]2 = (5.0 × 10−3)(5.0 × 10−1) = 2.5 × 10−3, giving [NO2] = 5.0 × 10−2 mol dm−3.

Products go on top of the K<sub>c</sub> expression, each raised to its coefficient. O<sub>2</sub> (power 5) and NH<sub>3</sub> (power 4) are products, while NO (power 4) and H<sub>2</sub>O (power 6) are reactants: 4NO + 6H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ 4NH<sub>3</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub>.

Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (1 mol N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> vs 2 mol NO<sub>2</sub>), shifting right. Because the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium left.
A larger volume lowers the pressure, so the equilibrium shifts to the side with more gas moles (2 mol on the right vs 1). SO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> decreases and Cl<sub>2</sub> increases.
N2O4 falls by 0.25 mol, so NO2 rises by 0.50 mol to 1.50 mol (in 1.0 dm3). Kc = (1.50)2/0.75 = 3.0.

Temperature changes K (exothermic reaction), and pressure shifts the position because the gas moles change (4 → 1). A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but doesn't change the amount of X<sub>3</sub>Y.
The forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +14 kJ), so raising the temperature shifts equilibrium towards the products and K increases.

p1.key: Equilibrium vapour pressure depends only on temperature. Lowering the temperature lowers the vapour pressure; adding liquid or vapour, or changing the volume, only causes temporary changes.

p1.key: Higher pressure shifts equilibrium to fewer gas moles (4 → 2), increasing NH<sub>3</sub>. The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising temperature decreases the yield. A catalyst does not shift the position of equilibrium.
Removing CO<sub>2</sub> shifts the equilibrium to the left, using up H<sup>+</sup>. [H<sup>+</sup>] falls, so pH increases.
Reversing a reaction inverts K: K = 1/0.25 = 4.0.
A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the yield of SO<sub>3</sub> and ΔH are unchanged.

Vaporization is endothermic, so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium towards vapour. At the new equilibrium the rates of vaporization and condensation are equal again, but there is more vapour than before.

Removing O<sub>2</sub> (a product) shifts equilibrium right (II). Increasing the volume lowers the pressure, favouring the side with more gas moles (3 vs 2), also right (III). A catalyst does not shift equilibrium.

K<sub>c</sub> increases with temperature, so raising T favours the forward reaction, which must be endothermic. K<sub>c</sub> stays below 1 even at 900 K, so the reaction does not go nearly to completion.
The reverse reaction always has the opposite ΔH: −210 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, but the concentrations need not be equal or in any fixed ratio.
K<sub>c</sub> depends only on temperature. Changing the concentrations does not change K<sub>c</sub> (here the new ratio 0.4 × 0.4/0.4<sup>2</sup> = 1 is the same as 0.2 × 0.2/0.2<sup>2</sup> = 1).

Forward reaction: 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas and exothermic. Higher pressure favours fewer gas moles, lower temperature favours the exothermic direction, and adding O<sub>2</sub> shifts the position right. All three increase SO<sub>3</sub> yield.
Kc = [Fe(CNS)²⁺] ÷ ([Fe³⁺][CNS⁻]), so units = (mol dm⁻³) ÷ (mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³.

The forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature shifts equilibrium right, increasing SO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>. Larger volume (lower pressure) favours the side with more gas moles (left); a catalyst does not shift the position.

The forward reaction is exothermic (favoured by low temperature) and reduces gas moles from 4 to 2 (favoured by high pressure). So low temperature and high pressure maximize the equilibrium yield of NH<sub>3</sub>.

Equilibrium vapour pressure depends only on temperature. Warming to 308 K gives more molecules enough energy to escape, so vapour pressure rises. Adding liquid or changing the volume does not change it once equilibrium is re-established.
p1.flag: Vapour pressure is not explicit in the 2025 guide.

p1.key: The forward reaction reduces gas moles (3 → 2), so increasing pressure shifts equilibrium right, increasing [SO<sub>3</sub>]. Removing O<sub>2</sub> or raising T (exothermic forward) shifts it left; a catalyst does not change the position.

K<sub>c</sub> changes only with temperature. Raising the temperature shifts this exothermic equilibrium left and decreases K<sub>c</sub>. Pressure and concentration changes shift the position but K<sub>c</sub> stays the same; a catalyst changes neither.
At equilibrium the concentrations stay constant. At 10 s the curves cross but are still changing; by 20 s and at 55 s both lines are flat. C: II and III only.

Vaporization is endothermic, so raising the temperature shifts Br2(l) ⇌ Br2(g) to the right, increasing [Br2(g)]. Changing the amount of liquid does not change the vapour concentration, and decreasing the volume shifts the position back towards liquid. D.
The second equation is the first reversed and halved. Reversing gives 1/Kc1; halving takes the square root: Kc2 = (1/Kc1)½. So Kc1 = 1/Kc22.

Higher temperature speeds up both forward and reverse reactions. More Cl2 at equilibrium means the forward (endothermic) reaction is speeded up more than the reverse, until the rates are equal again. C.

The equilibrium vapour pressure depends only on temperature. Surface area, the amount of liquid and the container volume change how fast equilibrium is reached or how much evaporates, but not the final vapour pressure.

At equilibrium the rate of dissolving equals the rate of crystallizing, so the solution concentration (colour) stays constant. Ions keep leaving and rejoining the crystal, so its shape may change. The flask is stoppered, so no water evaporates. D.
Vaporization is endothermic. Lowering the temperature favours the exothermic reverse change, so the position shifts to the left and Kc = [CH3OH(g)] decreases. Only temperature changes the value of K.
The forward reaction is endothermic, so increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium right, giving more CO2. There are 6 mol of gas on each side, so pressure has no effect.
Forming 0.80 mol IBr uses 0.40 mol each of I2 and Br2, leaving 0.10 mol of each. Kc = 0.802/(0.10 × 0.10) = 64 (the volume cancels because the number of moles is equal on both sides).
The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −128 kJ). Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left, so the yield of CH3OH decreases and K decreases.

"Dynamic" means the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so reactants and products keep reacting even though concentrations stay constant. The position and concentrations do not change at equilibrium.

Fewer gas moles on the right (4 → 2), so higher pressure shifts equilibrium to NH<sub>3</sub> and raises the yield, but high-pressure plant is expensive. Higher temperature lowers the yield (exothermic); lower temperature slows the rate.
At dynamic equilibrium forward and backward rates are equal, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant. They are not necessarily equal to each other.
Raising temperature always increases k (more collisions exceed Ea). For an exothermic reaction, higher temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left, so Kc decreases.

Starting with reactants only, the forward rate begins high (X) and falls to the equilibrium value (W–Z); the backward rate starts at zero (Y) and rises. Reactant concentration falls between Y and W, and at equilibrium the concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.

Heating shifts the endothermic liquid → vapour process to the right: more molecules have enough energy to escape, so the rate of vaporization and the vapour pressure increase, while the mass of liquid decreases.
The forward reaction is endothermic, so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium towards the products (absorbing heat), and Kc increases.

The forward reaction is endothermic, so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium right (more red). Adding FeCl<sub>3</sub> increases [Fe<sup>3+</sup>] and also shifts it right. A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
Kc = [N2O4] / [NO2]2 = 4.0 / (4.0)2 = 0.25. Forgetting to square [NO2] gives 1, and inverting the expression gives 4.0.

The forward reaction is exothermic. Lowering the temperature favours the exothermic direction, so the equilibrium shifts right. More products means Kc increases. Temperature is the only factor that changes K.
1.0 mol NOCl reacted, forming 1.0 mol NO and 0.50 mol Cl2 (in 1.0 dm3). Kc = [NO]2[Cl2] / [NOCl]2 = (1.0)2(0.50) / (1.0)2 = 0.50.
Kc falls as temperature rises, so the forward reaction is exothermic and lower temperatures favour HI. There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium.

Removing NH<sub>3</sub> pulls the equilibrium right. The forward reaction is exothermic, so lowering the temperature also favours it. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (2 vs 4), which is also the right.

A very large Kc means the products dominate at equilibrium, so the reaction goes almost to completion. K says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached, and at equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal.

Shifting right on heating requires an endothermic forward reaction (B or D). Shifting left at higher pressure requires more gas moles on the product side: N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (1 mol) → 2NO<sub>2</sub> (2 mol). In D the products have fewer moles.
3.0 mol HI forms from 1.5 mol each of H2 and I2, leaving 0.5 mol of each in 1.0 dm3. Kc = [HI]2/([H2][I2]) = (3.0)2/(0.5)2 = 36.

There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so changing the volume (pressure) does not shift the equilibrium. Kc depends only on temperature, so it remains unchanged. The H2 concentration actually increases as the volume decreases (A wrong).
The forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours SO3. There are 3 mol gas on the left and 2 on the right, so high pressure also shifts equilibrium to the right.
At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal (not zero) and the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant, but they are not usually equal to each other.
The forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −18.4 kJ), so raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction: the equilibrium moves left and Kc decreases. Only temperature changes Kc.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising T shifts the equilibrium to the endothermic side, the left. Higher temperature increases the rates of both forward and reverse reactions.
CO reacted = 0.40 − 0.25 = 0.15 mol, so H2 reacted = 2 × 0.15 = 0.30 mol, leaving 0.10 mol H2, and 0.15 mol CH3OH formed.

The forward reaction is endothermic, so raising T shifts it right (I). The right side has more gas molecules (2 vs 1), so lowering pressure shifts it right (II). A catalyst speeds up both directions equally and does not move the position (III).
Kc changes only with temperature. Concentration and pressure changes shift the position of equilibrium but not K, and a catalyst affects neither.
ΔH = +26 kJ mol−1, so dissolving is endothermic. By Le Châtelier's principle, raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so solubility increases at higher temperature.
Kc = [H2S]2 ÷ ([H2]2[S2]) = 1.075 × 108 ≫ 1, so [H2S]2 > [H2]2[S2] always. The individual concentrations in B and C depend on starting amounts.
CO2(g) is the only gas, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right (fewer gas molecules). More H+(aq) forms, so the pH decreases.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing T shifts the equilibrium to the left. [H+] falls, so the pH increases (and more CO2 gas is released).
N2 falls by 0.2 mol dm−3, so H2 falls by 3 × 0.2 = 0.6 → 0.4, and NH3 rises by 2 × 0.2 = 0.4 → 1.4 mol dm−3.

A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position does not change. Volume, pressure and temperature changes all shift this equilibrium because the moles of gas change and ΔH ≠ 0.
There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so changing pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium. Kc depends only on temperature, which is constant, so Kc stays the same.

Kc increases as temperature rises, so the equilibrium shifts to the right at higher temperature: the forward reaction is favoured (it is endothermic). At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are always equal, so C is wrong.
The new reaction is the reverse of the given one (invert K) and halved (take the square root). K = (1/7.3 × 1034)½ = 1/√(7.3 × 1034).

The left has 3 mol of gas and the right has 4 mol, so decreasing pressure shifts equilibrium right (towards more gas molecules). The forward reaction is endothermic, so cooling would shift it left; adding NO or removing O2 also shifts it left.
0.10 mol dm−3 of each of I2 and Br2 reacted, forming 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 mol dm−3 IBr. K = [IBr]2/([I2][Br2]) = 0.202/(0.10 × 0.10) = 4.
Kc depends only on temperature; pressure changes do not affect it. The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising the temperature shifts equilibrium left and Kc decreases.
A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the position and K<sub>c</sub> are unchanged. Only temperature changes K.
Only temperature changes K. The forward reaction is exothermic, so decreasing the temperature shifts equilibrium to the right and increases Kc. Changing concentrations shifts the position but not K.
Reversing the reaction gives 1/K = 1/4.0 = 0.25; halving the coefficients takes the square root: K = √0.25 = 0.50.
Forming 0.80 mol IBr uses 0.40 mol each of I2 and Br2, leaving 0.10 mol of each. Volume cancels (equal moles on each side): Kc = 0.802/(0.10 × 0.10) = 64.

Adding NaCl increases [Cl<sup>−</sup>], so equilibrium shifts right to use it up (common-ion effect). Removing solid AgCl has no effect; adding water dilutes the ions (shifts left); pressure has no effect without gases.
ΔG° = −RT ln K. If the reverse reaction is favoured, K < 1, so ln K is negative and ΔG° is positive.
